series: Capability-relevant events to mark on the charts
unit: none (value is null for every event)
description: Dated events, each with a type: architecture, training recipe, scaling, release event (a company releasing or announcing a result, often developed privately, all at once), plus three extra types used here: measurement (a change in how a chart's metric is computed or published), demonstration (a third party using a released model), claim (a public claim later withdrawn). release_event is true where a chart jump, or a result with no chart point, coincides with a company disclosing something it had developed out of view; dump is true for the Oct 6, 2026 math release.
license: Compiled for this post from the cited sources; facts only.
caveats: Release events mark disclosure dates, not development dates: a jump at a release event says when the public learned of a capability, so it overstates the speed of change at that moment and understates it before.
Several 2026 events concern unreleased models whose compute, attempts and failure counts are undisclosed; they cannot be placed on a capability curve.
Items marked (v) were taken secondhand (press, Wikipedia, or the post's own research files) rather than from the primary page.

points.note: Five-game match Mar 9 to 15, 2016, won 4 to 1. Policy and value networks trained on human games, then improved by self-play reinforcement learning against the game result: the canonical answer-key domain.
points.label: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol

points.model: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" (Google)
points.note: arXiv v1 June 12, 2017. The architecture behind every model in these charts.
points.label: Transformer

points.note: Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute: steady improvement that is diminishing returns written as a formula.
points.label: Neural scaling laws

points.note: arXiv v1 May 28, 2020. Few-shot ability from scale alone. METR dates its davinci-002 stand-in to this day (0.14 min horizon).
points.label: GPT-3

points.note: Blog post Jan 27, 2022; paper (Ouyang et al.) arXiv v1 Mar 4, 2022. Fine-tuning on human demonstrations and human preference rankings (RLHF): people become the grader, the recipe behind every chatbot since.
points.label: InstructGPT / RLHF

points.note: Hoffmann et al.: for a fixed compute budget, train smaller models on more data; resets the scaling recipe.
points.label: Chinchilla (compute-optimal scaling)

points.note: Public release of an RLHF chat model; the start of mass use, not a capability jump on these benchmarks.
points.label: ChatGPT

points.note: Released Mar 14, 2023 (technical report arXiv 2303.08774). The anchor model for the LMArena gap in preference.json and a METR point (4.0 min, TH1.1).
points.label: GPT-4

points.note: First public Elo leaderboard (open models only); proprietary models first appear in the May 8, 2023 snapshot.
points.label: Chatbot Arena leaderboard starts

points.note: Per LMArena's dataset notes; the space snapshot files label ratings "bt" from Dec 6, 2023. The scale is relative either way.
points.label: Arena switches from Elo to Bradley-Terry

points.note: Reinforcement learning against automatically checked answers (math, code), with long chains of thought. Release event: the method was developed privately before release (reported as Q* in Nov 2023 and "Strawberry" in July 2024 by Reuters (v)), and the benchmark jump arrives on release day: Epoch MATH Level 5 53% to 89%, OTIS Mock AIME 10% to 47%.
points.label: o1: reasoning via reinforcement learning

points.note: Announced and scored by the ARC Prize on the semi-private set; the model was not released until Apr 16, 2025, and the released o3 scored lower (60.8% at high effort, 53.8% at medium, per Epoch's copy of the ARC Prize leaderboard).
points.label: o3 announced (ARC-AGI-1 75.7%, 87.5% at high compute)

points.note: Open weights and a published method (paper arXiv 2501.12948, Jan 22, 2025): RL against automatic checks of math and code, four months after o1. The answer-key strength is easy to copy.
points.label: DeepSeek-R1: the reasoning recipe goes public

points.note: Defines the 50% time horizon; reports doubling about every 7 months, 2019 to 2025.
points.label: METR time-horizon metric published

points.note: Default leaderboard now discounts length and formatting effects; offset adjusted to keep the scale comparable (LMArena).
points.label: Arena makes style control the default

points.model: OpenAI experimental reasoning model; Gemini Deep Think (Google DeepMind)
points.note: OpenAI announced its result on July 19, 2025 (v, social-media post, not fetched); Google DeepMind's officially graded gold-medal result was announced July 21, 2025. Both were unreleased systems.
points.label: Gold-medal score at the IMO by unreleased models

points.note: OpenAI researchers posted that GPT-5 had solved ten open Erdos problems; erdosproblems.com's Thomas Bloom replied that "open" meant he knew no paper, and GPT-5 had found existing papers. Posts deleted (date Oct 17 or 18 per sources). A literature search, not new proofs.
points.label: GPT-5 "solved ten Erdos problems" claim withdrawn

points.note: Announced with Project Glasswing; Anthropic: it does "not plan to make Claude Mythos Preview generally available"; access limited to partners and vetted security organizations. METR's last and highest point (early version, at least 16 h, a lower bound).
points.label: Claude Mythos Preview announced, not generally released

points.note: A disproof of Erdos's 1946 conjecture, checked by outside mathematicians in a companion paper (Alon, Bloom, Gowers, Litt, Sawin, Shankar, Tsimerman, Wang, Wood). OpenAI's announcement page could not be fetched here (blocked) and is cited from the post's research files (v).
points.label: Unreleased OpenAI model disproves the unit distance conjecture

points.note: Corrected errors affecting 42% of problems; v1 and v2 scores are not comparable.
points.label: FrontierMath v2

points.note: Page notice: "no longer actively updated." Last model added May 8, 2026 (Claude Mythos Preview early). Measurements above 16 hours were already flagged unreliable.
points.label: METR stops updating its time-horizon page

points.note: Announced at noon Sept 8, 2026. Per OpenAI's post as summarized by Wikipedia (v): at least 10,000 agents, an 88-hour run from Sept 1, 2.7 million messages, 130 billion output tokens; Noam Brown: "this result cost millions of dollars." It addresses the version with an external force; specialists and Scientific American (Sept 21) say the unforced problem is still open, and Clay lists it as open.
points.label: OpenAI claims Navier-Stokes (forced version)

points.model: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), run by Carter Church (SentinelOne)
points.note: About six hours to transcribe and break the cipher, per Church (Euronews, Oct 2, 2026). A user-run demonstration with a released model.
points.label: GPT-6 Astra decodes an 1809 cipher letter to Marmont

points.note: OpenAI posted 722 mathematics manuscripts to GitHub; about 4,000 problems posed; "three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking" per kept result on average; about 42% of top-line results Lean-formalized (README); three withdrawn Oct 7 over one sign error (catalogue now 719). Total attempts, compute, prompts and model undisclosed. Released all at once: a dump of results produced over the preceding weeks (manuscripts dated mostly Sept 23 to 27 per the repository's CONTENTS.md, counted in the post's research notes), not a measured point on any curve.
points.label: The math dump: 722 manuscripts in an afternoon

points.note: In under half an hour, showed the P-192 to P-521 seeds came from a 1990s C-library random-number routine seeded by a clock reading; reproduced by Filippo Valsorda (bounty organizer). One seed remains unexplained per the post's research notes.
points.label: Anthropic model explains the NIST elliptic-curve seeds
